plain_english: Everyone enjoys reading a book more when it's written in clear, beautiful handwriting. In the same way, people listen more carefully when you use the right words that fit what you're saying. So don't claim that speaking well doesn't matter. That's what godless and cowardly people say. Godless because they dismiss the gifts God gave us — like claiming vision or hearing are worthless. Did God give you eyes for no reason? Did he waste his time putting such powerful and skillful energy into them that they can see far distances and make sense of what they see? What messenger moves as fast and stays as alert as your vision? Did he pointlessly make the air so effective and flexible that your sight can pass right through it? Did he create light for no reason, when without it nothing else would work? Don't be ungrateful for these gifts, but don't forget about the even greater things either. Yes, be thankful to God for your ability to see and hear, for life itself, and for everything that keeps you alive — dried fruits, wine, and oil. But remember: he gave you something better than all of these. He gave you the power to use them, test them, and figure out what each one is worth.
original_excerpt:
Every man will read a book with more pleasure or even with more ease, if it is written in fairer characters. Therefore every man will also listen more readily to what is spoken, if it is signified by appropriate and becoming words. We must not say then that there is no faculty of expression: for this affirmation is the characteristic of an impious and also of a timid man. Of an impious man, because he undervalues the gifts which come from God, just as if he would take away the commodity of the power of vision, or hearing, or of seeing. Has then God given you eyes to no purpose? and to no purpose has he infused into them a spirit so strong and of such skilful contrivance as to reach a long way and to fashion the forms of things which are seen? What messenger is so swift and vigilant? And to no purpose has he made the interjacent atmosphere so efficacious and elastic that the vision penetrates through the atmosphere which is in a manner moved? And to no purpose has he made light, without the presence of which there would be no use in any other thing?

Man, be neither ungrateful for these gifts nor yet forget the things which are superior to them. But indeed for the power of seeing and hearing, and indeed for life itself, and for the things which contribute to support it, for the fruits which are dry, and for wine and oil give thanks to God: but remember that he has given you something else better than all these, I mean the power of using them, proving them, and estimating the value of each.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: What is it that judges each of these abilities? What tells you what each one is worth? Does each ability judge itself? Have you ever heard your eyesight comment on itself? Or your hearing? Or wheat, barley, a horse, or a dog? No. They're all servants. They serve the one ability that can use what your senses show you. And when you ask what something is worth, who do you ask? Who gives you the answer? So how could any other ability be more powerful than this one? This one uses all the others as servants. It tests them and makes judgments about them. Which of your other abilities knows what it is or what it's worth? Which one knows when to work and when to stop? What makes your eyes open and close? What turns them away from things they shouldn't look at and toward things they should? Is it your eyesight? No. It's your will.
original_excerpt: For what is that which gives information about each of these powers, what each of them is worth? Is it each faculty itself? Did you ever hear the faculty of vision saying anything about itself? or the faculty of hearing? or wheat, or barley, or a horse, or a dog? No; but they are appointed as ministers and slaves to serve the faculty which has the power of making use of the appearances of things. And if you inquire what is the value of each thing, of whom do you inquire? who answers you? How then can any other faculty be more powerful than this, which uses the rest as ministers and itself proves each and pronounces about them? for which of them knows what itself is, and what is its own value? which of them knows when it ought to employ itself and when not? what faculty is it which opens and closes the eyes, and turns them away from objects to which it ought not to apply them and does apply them to other objects? Is it the faculty of vision? No, but it is the faculty of the will.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: What controls whether you listen or tune out? What makes you curious about some things but leaves you cold toward others? Is it just your ears? No. It's your will. Your will sits among all your other abilities — which are blind and deaf and can only do their basic jobs to serve your will. But your will alone sees clearly. It judges what each ability is worth. So will your will tell you that something else is most important? Or that it itself is? What does your eye do except see when you open it? But who decides whether you should look at someone's wife, and how you should look? Your will decides. Who decides whether to believe what you hear, and whether to let it affect you? Your will.
original_excerpt: What is that faculty which closes and opens the ears? what is that by which they are curious and inquisitive, or on the contrary unmoved by what is said? is it the faculty of hearing? It is no other than the faculty of the will. Will this faculty then, seeing that it is amidst all the other faculties which are blind and dumb and unable to see anything else except the very acts for which they are appointed in order to minister to this (faculty) and serve it, but this faculty alone sees sharp and sees what is the value of each of the rest; will this faculty declare to us that anything else is the best, or that itself is? And what else does the eye do when it is opened than see? But whether we ought to look on the wife of a certain person, and in what manner, who tells us? The faculty of the will. And whether we ought to believe what is said or not to believe it, and if we do believe, whether we ought to be moved by it or not, who tells us? Is it not the faculty of the will?
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: But if you ask me what the most excellent thing is, what should I say? I can't say it's the power of speaking. It's the power of the will, when it's set right. This is what controls your speaking power and all your other abilities, big and small. When your will is set right, a bad person becomes good. When it fails, a person becomes bad. This is why we're unlucky or lucky. This is why we blame each other or are pleased with each other. In short, if we ignore our will, we become unhappy. If we take careful care of it, we become happy.
original_excerpt: But if you ask me what then is the most excellent of all things, what must I say? I cannot say the power of speaking, but the power of the will, when it is right ([Greek: orthae]). For it is this which uses the other (the power of speaking), and all the other faculties both small and great. For when this faculty of the will is set right, a man who is not good becomes good: but when it fails, a man becomes bad. It is through this that we are unfortunate, that we are fortunate, that we blame one another, are pleased with one another. In a word, it is this which if we neglect it makes unhappiness, and if we carefully look after it, makes happiness.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english:
What usually happens? People act like travelers who find a nice inn on the way home. They like it so much they decide to stay there. But you've forgotten your purpose — you weren't traveling to the inn. You were just passing through it. "But this is such a pleasant inn!" Sure. And how many other inns are pleasant? How many meadows are beautiful? They're all just for passing through. Your real purpose is to get home, to ease your family's worries, to do your civic duties, to marry, have children, and serve in public office. You didn't come here to pick out the most pleasant spots. You came to live where you were born and where you're a citizen.

The same thing happens with philosophy. You use speech and the lessons you get here to move toward perfection. You purge your will and fix the part of your mind that deals with how things appear to you. Teaching requires a certain way of speaking — with variety and sharpness. But some people get captivated by these very tools. One person falls in love with elegant expression. Another gets obsessed with logical arguments. Another with clever tricks of reasoning. Another with some other roadside attraction. They stay there and waste away, like sailors trapped by sirens.
original_excerpt: What then is usually done? Men generally act as a traveller would do on his way to his own country, when he enters a good inn, and being pleased with it should remain there. Man, you have forgotten your purpose: you were not travelling to this inn, but you were passing through it. But this is a pleasant inn. And how many other inns are pleasant? and how many meadows are pleasant? yet only for passing through. But your purpose is this, to return to your country, to relieve your kinsmen of anxiety, to discharge the duties of a citizen, to marry, to beget children, to fill the usual magistracies. For you are not come to select more pleasant places, but to live in these where you were born and of which you were made a citizen. Something of the kind takes place in the matter which we are considering. Since by the aid of speech and such communication as you receive here you must advance to perfection, and purge your will and correct the faculty which makes use of the appearances of things; and since it is necessary also for the teaching (delivery) of theorems to be effected by a certain mode of expression and with a certain variety and sharpness, some persons captivated by these very things abide in them, one captivated by the expression, another by syllogisms, another again by sophisms, and still another by some other inn ([Greek: paudocheiou]) of the kind; and there they stay and waste away as they were among sirens.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: Your job was to learn how to handle life's events naturally. To get what you want without being crushed when you don't get it. To avoid what you dislike without falling into what you're trying to escape. To never feel unlucky or cursed. To be free — not blocked, not forced, not pushed around. To accept how Zeus runs the world. To obey willingly and be satisfied with it. To blame no one. To accuse no one of wrongdoing. To say from your heart: Lead me, Zeus, and you too, Destiny.
original_excerpt:
Man, your purpose (business) was to make yourself capable of using conformably to nature the appearances presented to you, in your desires not to be frustrated, in your aversion from things not to fall into that which you would avoid, never to have no luck (as one may say), nor ever to have bad luck, to be free, not hindered, not compelled, conforming yourself to the administration of Zeus, obeying it, well satisfied with this, blaming no one, charging no one with fault, able from your whole soul to utter these verses:

Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: Someone once said to Epictetus: "I've often wanted to hear you speak and come to visit you, but you never answered me. Please, if you can, say something to me now." Epictetus replied: "Do you think there's skill involved in speaking, just like there's skill in everything else? The person with skill speaks well, and the person without skill speaks poorly?" "Yes, I think so," the person said. "So the person who benefits himself and helps others when he speaks — he's skilled at speaking. But the person who harms himself and others when he speaks — he lacks this skill, right? You'll find that some people are hurt by speaking and others are helped by it. And are all listeners helped by what they hear? Or do you find that some listeners benefit and some are harmed?" "Both," the person said.
original_excerpt: TO (OR AGAINST) A PERSON WHO WAS ONE OF THOSE WHO WERE NOT VALUED (ESTEEMED) BY HIM.—A certain person said to him (Epictetus): Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer; and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me. Do you think, said Epictetus, that as there is an art in anything else, so there is also an art in speaking, and that he who has the art, will speak skilfully, and he who has not, will speak unskilfully?—I do think so.—He then who by speaking receives benefit himself, and is able to benefit others, will speak skilfully; but he who is rather damaged by speaking and does damage to others, will he be unskilled in this art of speaking? And you may find that some are damaged and others benefited by speaking. And are all who hear benefited by what they hear? Or will you find that among them also some are benefited and some damaged? There are both among these also, he said.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: So the people who listen well benefit, and the people who listen poorly get hurt? He agreed. Is there a skill to listening, just like there's a skill to speaking? It seems like it. If you want, think about it this way. Music — who does that belong to? A musician. Making a statue properly — who do you think that belongs to? A sculptor. And looking at a statue skillfully — does that seem like it needs no art? That needs art too. So if speaking well is the job of a skilled person, do you see that listening with benefit is also the job of a skilled person? Now, about speaking and listening perfectly and usefully — let's drop that topic for now, if you don't mind. Both of us are nowhere near that level. But I think everyone will agree on this: anyone who's going to listen to philosophers needs some practice in listening. Don't you think so?
original_excerpt: In this case also then those who hear skilfully are benefited, and those who hear unskilfully are damaged? He admitted this. Is there then a skill in hearing also, as there is in speaking? It seems so. If you choose, consider the matter in this way also. The practice of music, to whom does it belong? To a musician. And the proper making of a statue, to whom do you think that it belongs? To a statuary. And the looking at a statue skilfully, does this appear to you to require the aid of no art? This also requires the aid of art. Then if speaking properly is the business of the skilful man, do you see that to hear also with benefit is the business of the skilful man? Now as to speaking and hearing perfectly, and usefully, let us for the present, if you please, say no more, for both of us are a long way from everything of the kind. But I think that every man will allow this, that he who is going to hear philosophers requires some amount of practice in hearing. Is it not so?
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: Why don't you say anything to me? Here's what I can tell you: If you don't know who you are, why you exist, what this world is, who you're connected to, what's good and bad, beautiful and ugly — if you can't understand reasoning or proof, can't tell truth from lies — then you won't want the right things or avoid the right things. You won't move toward what's good or make plans or agree or disagree or hold back judgment properly. To put it simply: you'll stumble through life deaf and blind, thinking you're somebody important when you're really nobody. Is this happening for the first time? Haven't all human mistakes and disasters come from exactly this kind of ignorance since people first existed?
original_excerpt: Why then do you say nothing to me? I can only say this to you, that he who knows not who he is, and for what purpose he exists, and what is this world, and with whom he is associated, and what things are the good and the bad, and the beautiful and the ugly, and who neither understands discourse nor demonstration, nor what is true nor what is false, and who is not able to distinguish them, will neither desire according to nature nor turn away nor move towards, nor intend (to act), nor assent, nor dissent, nor suspend his judgment: to say all in a few words, he will go about dumb and blind, thinking that he is somebody, but being nobody. Is this so now for the first time? Is it not the fact that ever since the human race existed, all errors and misfortunes have arisen through this ignorance?
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1

plain_english: This is all I have to say to you. And honestly, I don't even want to say this much. Why? Because you haven't inspired me to teach you. What should get me excited about teaching you, the way skilled riders get excited by good horses? Should I look at your body? You neglect it. Your clothes? They're fancy and soft. Your behavior and appearance? They're worthless. When you want to listen to a philosopher, don't tell him "You're not teaching me anything." Instead, show that you're worthy of hearing something — show that you're ready to learn. Then you'll see how you can motivate a teacher to really speak.
original_excerpt: This is all that I have to say to you; and I say even this not willingly. Why? Because you have not roused me. For what must I look to in order to be roused, as men who are expert in riding are roused by generous horses? Must I look to your body? You treat it disgracefully. To your dress? That is luxurious. To your behavior, to your look? That is the same as nothing. When you would listen to a philosopher, do not say to him, You tell me nothing; but only show yourself worthy of hearing or fit for hearing; and you will see how you will move the speaker.
source_reference: Discourses, On the Power of Speaking, Section 1
